intro: A court decision has turned Activision into a cash-takeover trade with a visible upside and a much less certain downside.

plays.title: Activision Blizzard / ATVI — Four dollars for the remaining risk
parts: Why Retail Is Here

What makes Activision so tempting is that the buyer can point to an actual price. Microsoft has agreed to pay $95 a share in cash. Activision closed Tuesday at $90.99 after a US judge rejected the Federal Trade Commission's request for a preliminary injunction. The remaining difference is $4.01, down from $12.30 at Monday's close. Someone buying now can imagine a tidy gain from waiting for a transaction already announced, negotiated and tested in court. The appeal is greatest precisely when the arithmetic looks easiest. The target's fallback value, and the length of time the buyer might have to finance a position, are much harder to calculate. [deal] [gap]
What Is Driving It

The US judge ruled on whether the FTC had shown enough to stop the acquisition while its challenge proceeds. The UK's Competition and Markets Authority separately indicated it would consider proposals to resolve its concerns. The distinction matters in cash terms. Tuesday's news removes a significant immediate obstacle in one jurisdiction and opens a possible route in another. It does not put $95 in anyone's brokerage account. The parties have a July 18 deadline under their agreement. Delay, appeal, the terms of a UK remedy or a decision to extend the agreement can change the expected return even if the parties continue to want the same deal. [deal] [gap]
The Social Signal

A Tuesday WallStreetBets thread on the judgment shows why a cash merger is a powerful retail story. Participants discussed the offer price and questioned why the buyer's shares might behave differently from the target's. One person referred to owning calls, a self-reported position that says nothing about aggregate order flow. The question about the two stocks is more useful than a vote count. An Activision shareholder is buying a claim on a stated cash payment if conditions are met. A Microsoft shareholder owns the acquirer, which must pay the purchase price and then earn an adequate return on it. Two people reading the same ruling can reasonably choose entirely different trades. [rd] [deal]
Historical Analog

Monday's close gives a compact example of how merger pricing works. The spread was broad enough to pay for significant uncertainty. Tuesday's court result narrowed it sharply in one step. The next buyer takes the remaining regulatory and timing risk for a much smaller dollar reward. If the path clears, another comparable price jump would require something other than the existing offer. If a new obstacle appears, much of Tuesday's advance may be exposed. An investor who sees the old chart as a momentum breakout should ask what mechanism could carry the cash claim meaningfully above the contracted price. The economics differ from a company beating earnings and revising its own profit potential upwards. [gap]
Smart Money View

Merger investors generally compare the present value of the cash offer with a probability-weighted range of outcomes if the transaction is delayed or fails. A formal probability cannot be extracted from the $4.01 spread without assumptions about the independent value of Activision, the time to payment and funding costs. The UK regulator's willingness to talk improves one input. The FTC's ability to pursue the matter and the approaching deadline affect others. A smaller investor can use the same framework without trying to match a fund's position size. A fund following several transactions can spread the risk of one adverse decision. A single short-dated call cannot. [deal] [gap]
When the Narrative Breaks

Track each jurisdiction separately and read the conditions on any proposed agreement. A timetable slipping beyond the option's expiry would break a timing trade even if Microsoft ultimately pays in full. A successful appeal or more burdensome regulatory conditions could reopen the question of completion and return some of the spread very quickly. If the shares rise close to $95 before those questions are resolved, the residual dollar gain becomes small relative to the loss on a reversal. That is a sensible point to trim rather than treating the last few cents as free money. The next decision should follow the legal process and the purchase terms, not another game's sales figures. [deal] [gap]

plays.title: Coinbase / COIN — An agreement replaces an expectation
parts: Why Retail Is Here

Cboe has amended spot bitcoin fund applications to include surveillance-sharing agreements with Coinbase. The July filings had already identified Coinbase as the intended partner. Agreement on terms is a step forward, and the shares closed Tuesday up 9.8% at $89.15. An investor can now see why the stock has moved in two stages. The first repriced the probability Coinbase would have a role. The second reduced doubt about the mechanics of that role. Neither stage establishes the revenue the exchange would earn, or whether US regulators will approve the proposed funds. [c11]
Where It Breaks

The test is what happens after the next filing that adds little beyond documentation. If the stock cannot build on $89.15 as bitcoin holds firm, some investors may have bought the agreement as the event they intended to sell. A final regulatory decision or evidence of incremental paying business is worth more than a repeated mention of Coinbase's name. The regulatory risk to the exchange's other activities belongs in the share valuation throughout. [c11]

plays.title: Target / TGT — Buying a retailer others have marked down
parts: Why Retail Is Here

The TD Ameritrade June report put Target among stocks bought by both the overall client group and its millennial customers. A retailer under pressure has a familiar recovery appeal. A household may continue to visit the store even if it postpones purchases that earn the merchant a better margin. That makes anecdotal reports of busy shops a poor substitute for information about the mix of the shopping basket. Target's share price found support after a June 13 low of $125.08, the broker noted. That level gives an investor a visible point at which the customers who bought weakness face another test. [td]
Where It Breaks

If the shares revisit the June low, look for improvements in margin and inventory turnover before calling the decline a bargain. Discounts can attract traffic at the expense of profit. A decisive break with deteriorating merchandise economics would weaken the value argument, while resilience through another weak consumer reading would suggest expectations had already fallen substantially. The broker's historical buying gives market context; it offers no commitment that those clients will defend the same level again. [td]

plays.title: Chinese equities / FXI — Cheap prices can mean weak pricing power
parts: Why Retail Is Here

Chinese producer prices fell 5.4% from a year earlier in June, while the consumer price index was flat year on year. One way to trade the news is to buy a broad Chinese equity fund in anticipation of easier policy. Falling inflation gives policymakers more room to support credit or consumption, and markets can start pricing that before households see a change. There is a competing earnings effect. A company selling into weak final demand may have to take lower prices at precisely the point an equity investor is looking for a recovery in profits. [china]
Where It Breaks

Look for signs that easing actually leads to stronger orders, credit demand or purchasing power. A policy announcement that lifts equities briefly while producer prices keep falling would leave much of the profit question unresolved. A large-cap index also has its own sector weights; it can rise on regulatory relief in one large holding even if conditions for industrial businesses keep worsening. Avoid treating that as a broad verdict on Chinese demand. [china]
